Random Forest (ranger)
Random forest prediction averages across (B) trees:
\[\hat{p}(x) = \frac{1}{B} \sum_{b=1}^{B} T_b(x)\]
where (B = 500).
Each tree is built using bootstrap samples and feature subsampling.
Gini impurity:
\[Gini = 1 - p^2 - (1 - p)^2\]
Best split:
\[s^* = \arg\min_s \text{Impurity}(s)\]

XGBoost (Gradient Boosted Trees)
Prediction is a sum of boosted trees passed through a sigmoid:
\[\hat{p}_i = \sigma(F(x_i)) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-F(x_i)}}\]
with:
\[F(x) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} f_k(x)\]
Boosting update:
\[F_t(x) = F_{t-1}(x) + \eta f_t(x)\]
Objective function:
\[\mathcal{L} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \ell(y_i, \hat{p}_i) + \sum_{k=1}^{K} \Omega(f_k)\]
Logistic loss:
\[\ell(y, \hat{p}) =
- \left[y \log(\hat{p}) + (1 - y)\log(1 - \hat{p})\right]\]
Regularization:
\[\Omega(f) = \gamma T + \frac{1}{2}\lambda \sum_{j=1}^{T} w_j^2\]
where (T) is the number of leaves.

The short version: your delivery delays almost always come from one of four choke points — demand forecasting, inventory positioning, warehouse flow, or carrier performance — and the fastest wins usually come from tightening handoffs and exposing hidden bottlenecks with data you already have.
Below is a structured breakdown you can use immediately, even without new tools or systems.

title: HW2zalenaaron
section: 🧭 What’s most likely causing your delays
text:
🧭 What’s most likely causing your delays
Every delivery delay traces back to one or more of these categories. Think of them as the “big four failure modes”:

1. Upstream forecasting + order spikes
When demand is higher or more variable than expected:

Items go out of stock
Orders queue up waiting for replenishment
Promised delivery dates become unrealistic

Signals this is happening: frequent backorders, sudden surges tied to promotions, or SKUs with long lead times.


2. Inventory placement + replenishment timing
Even if you have stock, it may be in the wrong place.

Too much inventory in slow regions
Too little in fast-moving regions
Replenishment cycles that are too slow or too rigid

Signals: orders shipping from distant warehouses, high transfer activity, or “split shipments.”


3. Warehouse throughput + picking/packing bottlenecks
This is the most common hidden culprit.

Picking queues build up at certain times of day
Packing stations become the bottleneck
Cutoff times are too late relative to carrier pickup windows

Signals: orders sitting in “processing” for hours, spikes in cycle time during peak hours, or overtime usage.


4. Carrier performance + handoff timing
Even perfect internal operations can’t compensate for:

Missed carrier pickups
Overloaded regional hubs
Inconsistent last‑mile partners

Signals: tracking shows “label created” or “in transit” for too long, or delays cluster by ZIP code or carrier.

title: HW2zalenaaron
section: 🛠 What to do next (ranked by speed of impact)
text:
🛠 What to do next (ranked by speed of impact)

1. Map your order-to-delivery timeline
You need a simple, brutally honest view of where time is actually being lost. Break it into:

Order received → order released
Released → picked
Picked → packed
Packed → carrier pickup
Carrier pickup → delivery

Whichever segment has the biggest variance is your real problem.


2. Tighten your release-to-pick window
Most companies release orders in large batches, which creates artificial peaks. Instead:

Release orders continuously or in smaller waves
Prioritize by carrier cutoff time, not FIFO
Auto-flag orders at risk of missing cutoff

This alone can cut same-day delays by 20–40%.


3. Move inventory closer to demand
If you have multiple warehouses or 3PLs:

Rebalance stock based on the last 90 days of order geography
Reduce long-distance shipments
Increase safety stock for SKUs with high variability

If you only have one warehouse:

Increase safety stock on your top 20% SKUs
Shorten replenishment cycles



4. Fix warehouse bottlenecks
Look for:

Picking congestion (too many orders in the same zone)
Packing station shortages
Slow printing or labeling steps
Manual QA steps that don’t add value

Quick wins:

Add a second packing lane during peak hours
Pre-kit common bundles
Use zone picking for high-volume SKUs



5. Hold carriers accountable with data
Carriers respond to data, not complaints. Track:

Pickup timeliness
Average transit time by service level
Delay clusters by region

If one carrier is consistently late:

Shift volume to another
Move your pickup window earlier
Negotiate service-level credits

To give you a precise roadmap for fixing delivery delays, we need to look at the three primary “friction points” in a logistics chain.

title: HW2zalenaaron
text:
1. Phase One: The Warehouse (Processing Time)
If orders are sitting “in-process” for more than 24 hours, the issue is internal.

What to Analyze: * Pick-to-Ship Lag: Time elapsed from order placement to label generation.

Inventory Accuracy: Are items being marked as “in stock” when they aren’t (leading to backorders)?

The Fix:

Batch Picking: Group orders by SKU rather than individual orders to reduce walking time.
Safety Stock Buffers: Increase stock levels for “Hero” products (top 20% of sales) to prevent stock-outs.

title: HW2zalenaaron
text:
2. Phase Two: The Transit (Carrier Performance)
If the package is leaving your facility on time but arriving late, the issue is external.

What to Analyze:

Carrier SLA Compliance: Compare the “Estimated Delivery” vs. the “Actual Delivery” per carrier.
The “Last Mile” Bottleneck: Identify specific zip codes or regions where delays are concentrated.

The Fix:

Carrier Diversification: If one carrier is consistently failing, split volume between 2-3 providers to create redundancy.
Zone Skipping: Ship in bulk to a local hub closer to the destination before injecting packages into the final delivery network.

title: HW2zalenaaron
text:
3. Phase Three: The Communication (Customer Perception)
Sometimes the delay isn’t the problem—the surprise is the problem.

What to Analyze:

WISMO Rate: “Where Is My Order” inquiry volume.
Buffer Accuracy: Is your website promising 3 days when the data shows 5?

The Fix:

Dynamic Lead Times: Update your checkout page to reflect real-world shipping speeds based on current carrier delays.
Proactive Alerts: Send an automated “We’re running behind” email before the customer reaches out.



Recommended Action Plan

Audit the “Dead Time”: Calculate the average hours an order spends in a “Pending” state vs. “In Transit.”
Pareto Analysis: Identify if 80% of your delays are caused by 20% of your products or one specific carrier.
Automate Notifications: If a package hasn’t seen a scan in 48 hours, trigger an internal alert to investigate.

If you can provide a CSV or a summary of your recent shipping logs (Order Date, Ship Date, Delivery Date, and Carrier), I can perform a much deeper analysis for you.

Descriptive Statistics

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from IPython.display import display, Markdown

# Load and prepare ESG data
url_2024 = "https://bcdanl.github.io/data/esg_proj_2024_data.csv"
esg_data = pd.read_csv(url_2024)

# Rename columns to match expected names (note: use actual column names from CSV)
esg_data = esg_data.rename(columns={
    "Environmental": "Environmental_Risk",   
    "Social": "Social_Risk",                
    "Governance": "Governance_Risk",      
    "Total_ESG": "Total_ESG_Risk"         
})

# Download and process stock data
stock_data = pd.read_csv("https://bcdanl.github.io/data/stock_history_2023.csv")
stock_data['Date'] = pd.to_datetime(stock_data['Date'])
stock_returns = stock_data.groupby('Symbol')['Close'].apply(
    lambda x: x.iloc[-1]/x.iloc[0] - 1
).reset_index().rename(columns={'Close':'Annual_Return'})

# Merge datasets
merged = pd.merge(esg_data, stock_returns, on='Symbol', how='inner')

# ESG Risk Profiles - Summary statistics
esg_summary = esg_data.agg({
    'Symbol': 'nunique',
    'Total_ESG_Risk': 'mean',
    'Environmental_Risk': 'mean',
    'Social_Risk': 'mean',
    'Governance_Risk': 'mean'

    'Symbol': 'Companies',
    'Total_ESG_Risk': 'Avg_Total_Risk',
    'Environmental_Risk': 'Avg_Environmental',
    'Social_Risk': 'Avg_Social',

}).to_frame().T

When comparing the various risk scores to each other, we see that they follow different types of data distribution.
Environmental risk has a right scew, so while most companies have a small environmental risk, the companies that do have a high environmental risk tend to have a disproportionately high risk.
Government risk has a low standard deviation, with most companies falling around 5.
Social risk has a higher standard deviation than government risk, and averages a bit higher at around 10.

It appears that ESG scores and average annual return are minimally correlated. text:
Conclusion
This analysis reveals nuanced relationships between ESG risks and financial performance. Surprisingly, environmental and social risks demonstrated weak positive correlations, potentially indicating under-pricing of risks. While total ESG risk showed minimal overall correlation to returns, the component-level analysis proves more valuable, particularly the right-skewed distribution of environmental risks highlighting significant outliers.The findings suggest ESG measurements are not a significant indicator of stock performance.

3.2 Unit of Observation
Each observation represents team-level pre-tournament aggregate data

title: Data Analytics Capstone Project
text:
3.3 Key Variables
Describe your outcome variable, main explanatory variables, and important control variables.
The outcome variable we are predicting for is win probability.
WinPct= Win percentage
AvgPoints= Average points
AvgOppPoints= Average Opponent Points
FG2_Pct= two-point percentage
FG3_Pct= three-point percentage
FT_Pct= free-throw percentage
OR_pg= Offensive rebounds per game
DR_pg= Defensive rebounds per game
TO_pg= Turnovers per game
CareerTourneyWins= Coach’s historical success in previous tournaments, measured in number of NCAA tournament games won.
AdjEM= Adjusted efficiency margin, the number of points a team is expected to outscore the average D-1 team over 100 possessions
SOV= Strength of victory, average AdjEM percentile of opponents that a team defeated
AdjOE= Adjusted offensive efficiency, sourced from kenpom, points scored per 100 possessions and adjusted for opponent.
AdjDE= Adjusted defensive efficiency, points allowed per 100 possessions and adjusted for opponent.
RankAdjEM= Ranked adjusted efficiency margin, the number ranking of each team’s Adjusted efficiency margin each season
AdjTempo= Adjusted tempo, measured in possessions per 40 minutes and adjusted for opponent.

text:
3.4 Data Cleaning
Explain major cleaning steps, sample restrictions, missing values, and variable construction.
loading data into a directory


Code
data_dir <- "csvs"

files <- list.files(
  data_dir,

  full.names = TRUE

data <- files %>%
  set_names(tools::file_path_sans_ext(basename(.))) %>%
  map(~ tryCatch(

    }
  ))




Code
rs <- data$MRegularSeasonDetailedResults

team_games <- bind_rows(
  rs %>%
    transmute(
      Season, DayNum,
      TeamID = WTeamID, OpponentID = LTeamID,
      Win = 1, NumOT,
      Points = WScore, OppPoints = LScore,
      FGM = WFGM, FGA = WFGA, FGM3 = WFGM3, FGA3 = WFGA3,
      FTM = WFTM, FTA = WFTA,
      OR = WOR, DR = WDR,
      Ast = WAst, TO = WTO,
      Stl = WStl, Blk = WBlk,
      PF = WPF
    ),
  rs %>%
    transmute(
      Season, DayNum,
      TeamID = LTeamID, OpponentID = WTeamID,
      Win = 0, NumOT,
      Points = LScore, OppPoints = WScore,
      FGM = LFGM, FGA = LFGA, FGM3 = LFGM3, FGA3 = LFGA3,
      FTM = LFTM, FTA = LFTA,
      OR = LOR, DR = LDR,
      Ast = LAst, TO = LTO,
      Stl = LStl, Blk = LBlk,
      PF = LPF
    )
)

team_season_stats <- team_games %>%
  group_by(Season, TeamID) %>%
  summarise(
    Games = n(),
    WinPct = mean(Win),
    AvgPoints = median(Points),
    AvgOppPoints = median(OppPoints),
    FG2_Pct = sum(FGM - FGM3) / sum(FGA - FGA3),
    FG3_Pct = sum(FGM3) / sum(FGA3),
    FT_Pct = sum(FTM) / sum(FTA),
    ThreeP_Rate = sum(FGA3) / sum(FGA),
    OR_pg = median(OR),
    DR_pg = median(DR),
    Ast_pg = median(Ast),
    TO_pg = median(TO),
    Stl_pg = median(Stl),
    Blk_pg = median(Blk),
    PF_pg = median(PF),
    AvgOT = mean(NumOT),
    .groups = "drop"
  )




Code
kenpom_final <- data$kenpom_tournament_ready
# Filter to post-2002
team_season_stats <- team_season_stats %>%
  filter(Season >= 2003)




Code
# Strength of victories -----------------------------------------------------
# First, get the total number of teams per season for percentile calculation
teams_per_season <- kenpom_final %>%
  group_by(Season) %>%
  summarise(n_teams = n(), .groups = "drop")

# Prepare opponent KenPom ranks and join team count
opp_kenpom <- kenpom_final %>%
  select(Season, TeamID, Opp_RankAdjEM = RankAdjEM) %>%
  left_join(teams_per_season, by = "Season")

# Compute opponent percentile: (n_teams - rank + 1) / n_teams
opp_kenpom <- opp_kenpom %>%
  mutate(Opp_Percentile = (n_teams - Opp_RankAdjEM + 1) / n_teams) %>%
  select(Season, TeamID, Opp_Percentile)

# Join opponent percentiles to each game
team_games_with_opp <- team_games %>%
  left_join(opp_kenpom, by = c("Season", "OpponentID" = "TeamID"))

# Compute scaled SOV: average percentile of opponents that the team defeated
sov_scaled <- team_games_with_opp %>%
  filter(Win == 1) %>%
  group_by(Season, TeamID) %>%
  summarise(
    SOV_Scaled = mean(Opp_Percentile, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# coach feature -----------------------------------------------------------
# Get all coach data from MTeamCoaches
all_coaches <- data$MTeamCoaches %>%
  select(Season, TeamID, CoachName) %>%
  distinct() %>%
  arrange(CoachName, Season)

# Get tournament wins for each coach-season
tourney_wins <- data$MNCAATourneyDetailedResults %>%
  # Get primary coach for the winning team
  inner_join(
    data$MTeamCoaches %>%
      mutate(DaysCoached = LastDayNum - FirstDayNum + 1) %>%
      group_by(Season, TeamID) %>%
      arrange(desc(DaysCoached)) %>%
      dplyr::slice(1) %>%
      ungroup() %>%
      select(Season, TeamID, PrimaryCoach = CoachName),
    by = c("Season", "WTeamID" = "TeamID")
  ) %>%
  # Count wins per primary coach per season
  group_by(PrimaryCoach, Season) %>%
  summarise(SeasonWins = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  rename(CoachName = PrimaryCoach)

# Calculate coach career statistics (using ALL historical data)
coach_career_stats <- all_coaches %>%
  select(CoachName, Season) %>%
  distinct() %>%
  left_join(tourney_wins, by = c("CoachName", "Season")) %>%
  mutate(SeasonWins = coalesce(SeasonWins, 0)) %>%
  arrange(CoachName, Season) %>%
  group_by(CoachName) %>%
  mutate(
    # Career wins BEFORE current season
    CareerTourneyWins = lag(cumsum(SeasonWins), default = 0),
    # Years coached BEFORE current season
    YearsNCAA = row_number() - 1,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  select(CoachName, Season, YearsNCAA, CareerTourneyWins)

# Get primary coach for each team-season (for seasons >= 2003 to match team_season_stats)
primary_coaches <- data$MTeamCoaches %>%
  filter(Season >= 2003) %>%
  mutate(DaysCoached = LastDayNum - FirstDayNum + 1) %>%
  group_by(Season, TeamID) %>%
  arrange(desc(DaysCoached)) %>%
  dplyr::slice(1) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(Season, TeamID, CoachName)


Adding strength of victory, coach historical success, and Kenpom metrics to team season stats


Code
team_season_stats <- team_season_stats %>%
  left_join(
    kenpom_final %>% 
      select(Season, TeamID, AdjEM, AdjOE, AdjDE, AdjTempo, RankAdjEM) %>%
      mutate(TeamID = as.integer(TeamID)),
    by = c("Season", "TeamID")
  )

team_season_stats <- team_season_stats %>%
  # Remove any existing coach columns if they exist
  select(-any_of(c("CoachName", "YearsNCAA", "CareerTourneyWins"))) %>%
  # Join with primary coaches
  left_join(primary_coaches, by = c("Season", "TeamID")) %>%
  # Join with career stats
  left_join(coach_career_stats, by = c("CoachName", "Season")) %>%
  # Fill NA values with 0
  mutate(
    YearsNCAA = coalesce(YearsNCAA, 0),
    CareerTourneyWins = coalesce(CareerTourneyWins, 0)
  )

team_season_stats <- team_season_stats %>%
  left_join(sov_scaled, by = c("Season", "TeamID")) %>%
  rename(SOV = SOV_Scaled)
